meta.blurb: A lady with a mystery: her father vanished years ago, and now a pearl arrives in the post every year. Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson follow a trail of footprints, a clever little dog and a boat on the Thames to a treasure that men have killed for.
meta.bible: Sherlock Holmes: the consulting detective, bored without a puzzle, brilliant, vain, kind underneath. Dr John Watson: his friend and the narrator, a doctor who falls in love. Miss Mary Morstan: a young governess whose father vanished in 1878; calm and brave. Captain Arthur Morstan: her father, an army officer from India. Major John Sholto: his friend, who came home with a hidden treasure. Thaddeus Sholto: the Major's nervous, kind son. Bartholomew Sholto: his twin brother, killed at Pondicherry Lodge. McMurdo: the old boxer who guards the gate. Mrs Bernstone: the housekeeper. Athelney Jones: the confident Scotland Yard inspector. Toby: a small ugly dog with a perfect nose. Mr Sherman: the man who lends Toby, of Pinchin Lane. Mordecai Smith: owner of the steam launch Aurora. Jim Smith: his son. Jonathan Small: a man with a wooden leg, the thief and prisoner. Tonga: Small's small friend from the Andaman Islands. Abdullah Khan, Mahomet Singh and Dost Akbar: the three Sikh soldiers who join Small. Achmet: the merchant killed at Agra. The sign of the four: the four names signed on the old plan. The Agra treasure: a hoard of jewels. London, Upper Norwood, Pondicherry Lodge, the Lyceum Theatre, Baker Street, the Thames, Agra, India, the Andaman Islands, Worcestershire. Voice and tone: lively, clever and atmospheric, with a mystery that unrolls clue by clue and a story of greed and revenge told by the villain; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore; the last pages are warm and a little sad. Beat 50 closes with Watson and Mary together and Holmes alone.

A1A2: Holmes was bored without a case, and Watson worried about his health.
Holmes held Watson's watch and told him about his dead brother.
Then a young woman named Mary Morstan came to ask for help.
Her father, an army officer, had gone missing in London many years before.
Every year she got a large pearl in the post.
Now a new letter asked her to meet a friend at a theatre.
She also had her father's old paper with a plan and four names.
That evening they met at the theatre, and a man led them to a cab.
The cab drove for a long time through dark, wet streets.
A small bald man in a rich room said he knew her father's story.
He said that her father died after a fight with his own father.
Later his father died in fear after he saw a face at the window.
His brother Bartholomew found the treasure, and Thaddeus wanted Mary to have some.
At the big house, a huge old fighter named McMurdo opened the gate.
Bartholomew's door was locked, and nobody answered when they knocked.
They broke down the door and found Bartholomew dead in his chair.
A dark thorn was in his head, and a note lay beside him.
Holmes searched the room and then climbed up through a hole in the roof.
Holmes found small footprints, and the mark of a wooden leg.
Inspector Jones came and took Thaddeus away, but Holmes said that he was wrong.
Holmes went to a man named Sherman to borrow a clever dog.
The little dog followed the smell of tar through the streets of London.
Toby went to the river, and the trail ended at the water.
A woman said that her husband and his boat had gone the day before.
Holmes dressed as an old sailor, and the street boys searched the river.
Days passed with no news, and Watson often went to see Mary.
At last Holmes learned where the boat was, and the police came.
They saw the Aurora, and they began to chase her along the river.
The Aurora was very fast, but the police boat was faster.
A small, dark man on the boat lifted a long pipe, and they shot him.
The Aurora hit the mud, and the police caught a man with a wooden leg.
They opened the iron box at Baker Street, but it was empty.
Small said that he came from a farm and lost his leg to a crocodile.
A great war began in India, and Small ran to the fort at Agra.
In the fort, Small guarded a gate with three brave soldiers.
They killed a rich man, hid his treasure and drew a plan.
Later the four men were caught and sent to a prison on an island.
In the prison, Small told two army officers about the treasure.
Sholto took the treasure for himself and sailed away to England.
A small island man became Small's friend, and they escaped in a canoe.
In England, they found Sholto dead, and they went to his son's house.
Tonga climbed in through the roof, and his dart killed Bartholomew.
When the police chased them, Small threw the treasure into the river.
Small finished his story, and the police took him away.
Watson told Mary that the treasure was gone, but he was glad.
Then Watson told Mary that he loved her very much.
Mary smiled and said yes, and she gave him her hand.
Holmes said that he was pleased, but that he would never marry.
Inspector Jones got the praise, and Holmes sat alone and felt sad.
Watson went to his new life, and Holmes waited for the next mystery.
B1B2: Holmes always grew restless when he had no case to solve, and that afternoon he reached for a small bottle. Watson, who was a doctor, begged him to stop, because he knew that it harmed his friend's body and mind.

Holmes picked up Watson's old watch and described its owner: a careless man who had drunk too much and died poor. Watson was hurt, because the watch had belonged to his own brother, and he thought that Holmes had been spying.
Holmes said that nothing in the world was worse than a dull life, and he hoped that a puzzle would arrive soon. At that moment the maid announced a visitor, a young lady called Miss Mary Morstan.
Miss Morstan said that her father, an army captain in India, had come home to London in 1878. He had gone to meet an old friend, and since that day nobody had ever seen him again.
About six years earlier, an advertisement had asked her to write to a certain address. Since then a large, valuable pearl had arrived in the post every year, but nobody had signed a single letter.

That morning another letter had come, asking her to meet an unknown friend outside the Lyceum Theatre that evening. She might bring two friends but no police, and she asked Holmes and Watson to go with her.

She also showed them a paper that she had found among her father's belongings, a rough plan of a building with a cross on it. Beneath it were four names, Jonathan Small, Mahomet Singh, Abdullah Khan and Dost Akbar, and the words “the sign of the four.”

At seven o'clock they waited by the third pillar of the Lyceum, watching the crowds hurry past. A small man in a coachman's coat touched Mary's arm, led the three of them to a closed carriage and drove off at speed.
The cab rolled for miles through dark, foggy streets, and none of them could tell where they were. At last it stopped outside a plain house in a poor, quiet part of south London.

Inside, the rooms were full of rich carpets and curtains, and a small bald man with a nervous manner welcomed them. He was Thaddeus Sholto, and he said that he knew what had happened to Miss Morstan's father.

Thaddeus said that his father, Major Sholto, had come home from India with a great secret treasure. Captain Morstan had visited him to claim a share, and after a bitter argument he had suddenly fallen dead.
Years later the old Major lay dying, and he began to tell his sons where the treasure was hidden. Suddenly he saw a face at the window, screamed in terror and died before he could finish.

After years of searching, Thaddeus's brother Bartholomew had at last found the treasure hidden in the house. Thaddeus thought that it was only fair to give a share to Mary Morstan, so he asked them all to go to his brother's house.
At last they reached the dark gardens of Pondicherry Lodge, where a huge man named McMurdo, a former boxer, let them in. Holmes remembered him from a fight many years before.

The housekeeper, Mrs Bernstone, was frightened because Bartholomew had locked himself in his room and had not answered for hours. Thaddeus looked through the keyhole, saw something dreadful and fell back with a cry.
Holmes and Watson broke down the door and found Bartholomew Sholto dead in his chair, his face twisted into a terrible smile. The windows were closed, and the key was still in the lock on the inside.
Watson found a long, dark thorn stuck near the dead man's ear, and Holmes said that it was probably poisoned. On the table lay a paper with four words, “The sign of the four,” in an untidy hand.

Holmes examined the room with his magnifying glass, then climbed through a hole in the ceiling to the roof. He had decided that the murderer must have come and gone that way, not through the locked door.

Holmes found footprints that were very small and had no shoes, and beside them the round mark of a wooden stick. They were stained with a dark tar, and he said that two men had been there, one with a wooden leg.
Inspector Athelney Jones arrived with his men and, after a brief look, arrested Thaddeus Sholto for the murder. Holmes quietly told him that he was making a mistake, but Jones would not listen.
Holmes took Watson through the night to Pinchin Lane, where a man named Sherman kept many animals. He borrowed a small, ugly dog called Toby, which had the best nose for tracking in all London.

At Pondicherry Lodge Toby sniffed the tarry footprints, then trotted off with his nose to the ground. Holmes and Watson followed him for miles in the early light, past houses, shops and market stalls.
Toby once led them astray to a barrel of tar, but he soon found the trail again. It ended at the river, where the two men had clearly climbed into a boat.

Near the landing place, Holmes asked about boats and learned that a man named Mordecai Smith owned a fast steam launch called the Aurora. His wife said that he had left the day before with his son Jim, and she did not know when he would return.

Holmes came back to Baker Street dressed as a rough old sailor, and Watson did not know him until he laughed. He sent the street boys to search the whole river for the Aurora, and they were told to ask at every dock.
Several days went by without news, and Holmes grew restless in his chair. Watson visited Miss Morstan to tell her what had happened, and he found that he liked her more each time.

At last a message came: the Aurora had been seen near a boatyard on the south side of the river. Holmes, Watson and Inspector Jones climbed into a police launch and waited in the dusk for her to appear.
They saw the Aurora coming, with a tall figure at the wheel and a small shape in the bow. Jones shouted for her to stop, and the police launch leaped forward as the engineers piled on more coal.
For several miles the two boats raced along the river, throwing up great sheets of spray. The Aurora was fast, but the police launch slowly began to catch up.

A small, strange figure in the bow of the Aurora raised a long pipe to his lips, ready to blow a poisoned dart. Holmes and Watson fired their pistols together, and the little man fell into the dark water.
The Aurora ran onto a mudbank and stopped, and the man at the wheel, who had a wooden leg, was caught and tied up. In the little cabin the police found a heavy iron box that was locked.
The iron box was carried to Baker Street, where Mary Morstan waited in anxious silence. Watson broke the lock with a poker, and they found that the box was completely empty.
Small, who sat calmly with a cigar, said that he would tell the whole truth. He had been a farm boy from Worcestershire who joined the army and went to India, where a crocodile bit off his leg.
After his injury he became a manager on a plantation. When the great rebellion of 1857 began, he escaped with the other families to the fort at Agra.

In the fort, Small was ordered to guard a gate with three Sikh soldiers named Abdullah Khan, Mahomet Singh and Dost Akbar. They became firm friends, although they knew that terrible danger surrounded them.

One night a merchant named Achmet came to the gate, trying to hide a great treasure of jewels from the rebels. The four guards killed him, buried the treasure and drew a plan, which they signed with the sign of the four.
When the war ended, the four men were arrested for the crime and sentenced to prison on the Andaman Islands. Small was sure that he would die there, but he kept his secret.

The officers who watched the prisoners were Major Sholto and Captain Morstan, who loved to play cards. Small told them about the treasure and begged for their help to escape, promising that all would share.
Sholto, however, went to Agra without him, took the treasure for himself and sailed to England. Small decided that he would have his revenge, and he waited for years in prison.

Small made friends with a small islander named Tonga, who was sick and alone, and nursed him back to health. When the chance came, the two of them escaped in a canoe and were picked up by a passing ship.
They reached England at last, only to learn that Major Sholto was dead. They went to Pondicherry Lodge, where Bartholomew had found the treasure, and Tonga climbed up through the roof.

Tonga killed Bartholomew with a poisoned dart, and Small was shocked, because he had never wanted anyone to die. He wrote the note about the sign of the four, and then they carried the box to the Aurora.
When the police launch chased them, Small threw the box of jewels over the side into the deep river. If he could not have the treasure, he said, then nobody ever would.
Small finished his story, and nobody spoke for a while. Then the police took him away, still saying that he had been robbed far more than he had robbed anyone.
Later Watson told Mary that the treasure was gone for ever, and she did not seem upset. He found that he was glad, because without a fortune she was no longer far above him.
Watson took a deep breath and told Mary that he loved her, and that he had loved her since the first day. He said that he had been afraid to speak while she might be rich.
Mary smiled, took his hand and said that she loved him too. They sat together in happy silence, and for the first time in months Watson felt that he was no longer alone.
Holmes congratulated Watson in his dry way, and said that love was an emotional thing that spoiled cold reason. He added that he would never marry, in case it should spoil his judgement.
Inspector Jones took all the praise in the newspapers, and Holmes did not seem to mind much. He sat alone in the dusk with a paper and grumbled that life was dull without a puzzle.
Watson went off to his new life, and Holmes stood at the window of Baker Street, watching the rain. He knew that another strange problem would arrive soon, and he was ready for it.
C1C2: Without a problem to occupy him, Holmes sank into a restless gloom, and that afternoon he reached for the little bottle that Watson had long dreaded. The doctor protested, as he had protested many times before, that the habit was slowly wearing out both his friend's body and his remarkable mind. Holmes replied that what he could not bear was a dull, uneventful life, for he craved hard problems, hard work and the keenest puzzles.

Holmes took Watson's watch, studied the scratches round the keyhole and the marks left by a pawnbroker, and described its owner as a careless man who had once been well off and had died poor, a victim of drink. Watson, whose elder brother the watch had belonged to, flared with anger, believing that his friend had made cruel use of private papers. Holmes, who was truly sorry, explained that he had merely read the signs, and he offered a warm apology.

Holmes declared that a hard problem was the only thing that gave his life any meaning, and that he would gladly give a month's rest for a single mystery worth solving. As if the room had overheard him, a gentle knock sounded at the door, and a young governess, neatly dressed and quietly composed, was shown in. She introduced herself as Miss Mary Morstan and said that she had come in desperate need of advice.

Miss Morstan explained that her father, a captain in an Indian regiment, had returned to London on leave in 1878, and that she had hurried to meet him at his hotel. He had gone out the evening before to visit an old friend and had never come back, and no search or advertisement had ever turned up a trace of him. She had been left alone in the world, and had worked as a governess ever since.

Some six years ago, she told them, an advertisement had asked her to make herself known to a certain address, and she had answered it. Since then, a large and valuable pearl had arrived in the post on the same day every year, with no word to explain who had sent it or why. She had collected six pearls now, and she did not know whether to feel grateful or afraid.

That morning a new letter had come, written by an unknown hand, asking her to meet an unnamed friend outside the Lyceum Theatre that very evening. She might bring two friends, it said, but she must never bring the police, and the writer promised that she would be told something to her advantage. She laid the letter before Holmes and asked whether he and Watson would accompany her.

She also produced a yellowed paper that she had found among her father's belongings, a rough plan of a large building, with a cross drawn in one corner. Beneath it stood four names, Jonathan Small, Mahomet Singh, Abdullah Khan and Dost Akbar, and four words that sounded like a threat, the sign of the four. Holmes turned it over in his thin fingers, studied it with his lens and said nothing for a long time.

At seven o'clock they stood beneath the third pillar of the Lyceum, jostled by the evening crowd, until a small man in a coachman's coat touched Mary's arm and asked whether she had come with two friends. He led them to a closed carriage without another word, and the horses were whipped away at a gallop. The three of them, who had no idea where they were being taken, looked at each other in the gloom.

The carriage rattled for what seemed an age through the murky, gas-lit streets of London, and neither Watson nor Holmes could say with any certainty where they were. At last it came to a halt before a plain house in a poor, quiet district south of the river, and a servant in a turban opened the door. From within came a thin, nervous voice that begged them to come in and not to keep him waiting any longer.

The interior was a surprise, for the rooms were furnished with thick carpets, rich hangings and valuable pictures, and in the middle of this splendour sat a small, bald man with a worried face. He introduced himself as Thaddeus Sholto, asked Watson to examine his heart, and then declared that he knew exactly what had become of Miss Morstan's father. His hands shook as he said it, and he glanced behind him more than once.

Thaddeus explained that his father, Major John Sholto, had returned from India with a great hidden treasure, and that Captain Morstan had come to claim his share. The two old comrades had quarrelled bitterly, and in the middle of the argument Captain Morstan had been taken by a sudden heart attack and had fallen dead. The Major, terrified that nobody would believe him, had buried the secret along with the body.

Years later, as the old Major lay dying, he began to tell his two sons where the treasure was hidden, and then fell silent in horror as a face looked in at the window. He cried out that the man must not be let in, and a few minutes later he was dead, without finishing his sentence. In the morning, a scrap of paper was found lying on his chest, bearing the same four words that were on her father's plan.

After six years of fruitless searching, Thaddeus's brother Bartholomew had at last found the secret hiding place in the house at Pondicherry Lodge, and for a short while the two brothers had gazed together upon the whole glittering hoard. Thaddeus, feeling that it was only fair that Mary Morstan should receive her share, had sent her a pearl each year, and now he begged her to come to his brother's house that very night. He feared, however, that his twin would not agree to any such plan without some gentle and persistent persuasion.

The cab rolled up a long, dark drive and halted before the gates of Pondicherry Lodge, where an enormous old boxer named McMurdo let them through with a growl. Holmes, who had once fought him in a ring, had a quiet word with the man, and their grim host was suddenly all politeness. Beyond the trees, the great house stood silent, its windows dark and its garden full of shadows.

The housekeeper, Mrs Bernstone, met them at the door, wringing her hands and declaring that something terrible must have happened to Mr Bartholomew. He had locked himself in his room hours earlier, she said, and no knocking or calling had made any difference. Thaddeus, who had hurried to look through the keyhole, stepped back with a cry and sank against the wall.

Holmes and Watson put their shoulders to the door and broke it from its hinges, and there, in the middle of the room, sat Bartholomew Sholto in a high-backed chair. His head was thrown back, and his face was frozen in a hideous grin, while the windows were shut and the key sat in the lock on the inside. Watson, who had seen death in many forms, felt a shiver run through him.

Watson found a long dark thorn buried in the skin just above the dead man's ear, and Holmes, examining it carefully, declared that it was probably coated with some deadly poison. On the table lay a sheet of paper bearing four untidy words, the sign of the four, in a hand that Holmes had never seen before. Neither man could say how any assassin had entered a room that appeared to have been locked from within.

Holmes spent a quarter of an hour with his lens, crawling over the floor and examining the window, the door and every inch of the walls, before climbing through a small hole in the ceiling to the roof. When he came down he declared that the murderer had come and gone by that route, for the locked door had never been used. There was, he said, no other possible way into the room, and nothing else could explain what they had found.

On the roof beams and in the dust Holmes found the prints of tiny bare feet, so small that they might have belonged to a child, and beside them the round hole made by the end of a wooden leg. They were stained with a dark tar, and he said that two men had been there, one of them very strange and the other with a stick. Holmes, who was eager for the chase, rubbed his hands together with obvious pleasure and said that the trail would be easy to follow.

Inspector Athelney Jones arrived with his men, glanced round the room with an air of great self-confidence and promptly arrested Thaddeus Sholto and the housekeeper on suspicion of the murder. Holmes quietly told him that he was making a grave mistake, and that the real culprits were a man with a wooden leg and a small, barefoot companion. Jones, who was enjoying himself far too much to listen to anyone, only laughed and called for a cab.

Holmes took Watson through the night to a dingy house in Pinchin Lane, where a man named Sherman kept a dozen stuffed birds and many living animals, and roused him from his bed. From the clutter of cages he borrowed a small, ugly dog called Toby, which had the keenest nose for tracking in all London. Back at Pondicherry Lodge, the dog sniffed at the tarry footprints and wagged his tail.

Toby set off through the early morning streets with his nose to the ground and his tail wagging, and the two men followed him for miles, past silent houses, awakening shops and noisy market stalls. The smell of tar was strong enough for the dog but faint enough to be lost, and there were moments when Watson doubted that the chase could ever end. Holmes, who knew better than to doubt his borrowed bloodhound, simply strode on, and he did not once look back.

Once Toby went astray and led them to a barrel full of tar, but the little dog soon recovered himself and picked up the true trail again. It finished at the muddy edge of the Thames, where a landing place and a pile of planks showed that the two fugitives had boarded a boat. The tide had washed away everything else, and the river lay grey and indifferent before them.

Near the landing place Holmes asked after boats, and learned that a man named Mordecai Smith owned a fast steam launch called the Aurora, which was the swiftest on the river. His wife, a worried woman, said that he had left the day before with his son Jim, and she had no idea when he would be back. Holmes thanked her with a courteous bow and hurried away to plan his next move.

Holmes returned to Baker Street disguised as a hard-faced old sailor, so convincing that Watson did not recognise him until he burst out laughing. He sent Wiggins and the other street boys out to search every dock on the river for any sign of the Aurora, promising a handsome reward to whichever of them found her first. Then he settled into his armchair, filled his pipe and waited, with every appearance of calm, for news.

Several days went by without any sign, and Holmes grew more irritable and more restless with each passing hour. Watson, meanwhile, found that he had several good reasons to visit Miss Morstan, and he discovered that her quiet courage and her gentle smile pleased him more with every call. He did not dare to speak of what he felt, for she might still become a very rich woman.

At last a message arrived: the Aurora had been spotted near a boatyard on the south side of the river, and was likely to appear that evening. Holmes, Watson and Inspector Jones, who had given up arguing with Holmes, climbed aboard a police launch and waited in the dusk, the engine murmuring softly beneath them. As the lights began to prick the dark water, a long boat glided into view.

They saw the Aurora gliding out of the shadows, a tall figure at the wheel and a small shape crouched in the bow, and Jones bellowed for her to heave to. Instead the launch leaped forward as though she had been spurred, and the police engineers piled more coal on the fire so that sparks streamed from the funnel. The great chase had begun, and there was no longer any question of turning back or giving up.

For several miles the two boats flew along the river, hurling up great sheets of spray while the lights of the banks streamed past, and the Aurora kept ahead as only a fine, fast vessel can. Slowly, however, the heavier police launch began to gain, and the two crews could see each other's faces in the glow of the engine fires. The distance between them shrank to a few boat lengths, and every man on board held his breath.

From the bow of the Aurora the small, strange figure raised a long pipe to his lips and prepared to blow a poisoned dart at his pursuers. Holmes and Watson fired together, the sharp reports echoing across the water, and the little man gave a strangled cry and toppled backward into the dark river. Not a ripple remained to show where he had gone, and the night seemed very quiet for a moment.

The Aurora swerved, struck a mudbank and stuck fast, and in the confusion the man at the wheel, who had a wooden leg, was seized and bound. In the cramped cabin the police found a heavy iron box with a stout padlock, and Jones, who was delighted with his catch, ordered it carried carefully across to his own boat. The prisoner, whose name they now learned was Jonathan Small, sat quietly and said nothing at all.

They carried the iron box to Baker Street, where Miss Morstan waited in anxious silence, her hands clasped tightly in her lap. Watson, with no key to hand, smashed the lock with a poker, and when the lid flew open they saw that the box was completely empty. For a moment nobody spoke, until Mary said very quietly that she was glad.

Small, who sat comfortably with a cigar in his mouth as though he had nothing to fear, announced that he would tell them the whole truth, since he had little to lose. He had been a farm boy from Worcestershire, he said, who had joined the army and gone to India, where a crocodile had bitten off his leg as he swam in the Ganges. It was a great misfortune, but, as it turned out, only the first of many.

Discharged from the army, Small found work as a manager on an indigo plantation, and he was getting along well until, in 1857, the great rebellion broke out and the whole country seemed to burst into flames. He fled with the other families to the fortress at Agra, where he hoped that the stone walls would shelter him. As it proved, that was precisely the place where his real and lasting troubles were about to begin.

Because he was one of the few Englishmen who understood the people around him, Small was posted to guard a gate of the fort with three brave Sikh soldiers, Abdullah Khan, Mahomet Singh and Dost Akbar. In those anxious nights they became firm friends, knowing that the rebels might strike at any moment. Together, they would soon share a secret that bound them for the rest of their lives.

One dark night a merchant named Achmet appeared at the gate, carrying the hoard of a rebel prince, and asked for help in smuggling it to safety. The four guards were dazzled by the jewels, killed the poor man and buried the treasure beside a wall of the fort. Then they drew a plan and signed it with the sign of the four, and it was a crime that would haunt every one of them.

When the rebellion was at last crushed, the body was found, and the four men were arrested and sentenced to long years in prison on the distant Andaman Islands. Small, who had lost his leg and now lost his freedom, believed that he would die there. Yet he held on to his secret as a drowning man clings to a plank.

The guards on the island were Major Sholto and Captain Morstan, two officers who loved to play cards and who were often short of money. Small, who had watched them for years, at last told them about the treasure, and he begged them to help him escape. He promised that every man would be given his fair share, and they listened with growing interest.

But Sholto was a cunning man, and he betrayed the bargain, going to Agra without the others, taking the treasure for himself and sailing home to England as a wealthy man. When Small discovered what had happened, he swore that he would have his revenge. He nursed his hatred through many more years of captivity, and it grew stronger with every one of them.

In those years Small made friends with a small islander named Tonga, who had been wandering sick and alone in the jungle, and nursed him back to health with endless patience. When at last the chance came, the two of them slipped away in a canoe. They drifted for days before a passing ship picked them up and carried them towards England.

At last they reached England, only to learn that Major Sholto was already dead and that his sons were living at Pondicherry Lodge. Small and Tonga stood outside the dark house for a long time, studying the walls and the roof. Tonga, who could climb like a cat and had a taste for mischief, pointed upward at the roof and grinned broadly.

Tonga dropped through the hole in the roof and killed Bartholomew with a poisoned dart, a deed that horrified Small, who had never wished to take a life. He wrote the note about the sign of the four, as a final reminder of the old wrong, and left it beside the body. Then they carried the heavy treasure down to the waiting Aurora and set out into the darkness of the river.

When the police launch began to gain on them, Small seized the heavy box and heaved it over the side into the deep, dark water of the Thames. If he could not have the treasure, he declared, then no one else ever would. It had cost him a leg, a friend and twenty years of his life.

Small finished his story and sat back in silence, and for a while nobody in the room had anything to say. Then the police led him away into the night, and nothing could shake him. He insisted, to the very last, that he had been robbed far more than he had ever robbed anyone, and that justice had never once been on his side.

Later, in the quiet front room, Watson told Mary that the treasure was gone for ever, and she did not seem the least upset. He found, to his own surprise, that he was glad, because without a fortune she was no longer so far above his reach. It was a selfish thought, and he was ashamed of it, though not very much.

Taking a deep breath, Watson told Mary that he loved her, that he had loved her from the very first day, and that he had been afraid to speak while she might be rich. His voice faltered, and the carefully rehearsed words flew out of his head like startled birds. It was, he thought afterwards, the most difficult speech that he had ever attempted in his whole life.

Mary smiled, put her hand into his and told him that she loved him too, and that she had been waiting for him to say so. They sat together for a long while in a happy and contented silence, hardly needing words. For the first time since he returned from Afghanistan, Watson felt that he was no longer alone in the world.

Holmes congratulated them both in his own dry fashion, remarking that love was an emotional thing, and that whatever was emotional was opposed to the cold, true reason which he placed above everything. He added, with a slight smile, that he would never marry himself, for fear that it would warp his judgement. Watson, who knew his friend well, thought that he sounded a little sad when he said it.

In the newspapers, Inspector Jones took all the praise for the arrest, and Holmes, who had long ago stopped expecting thanks, did not seem to mind. He sat alone in the dusk with a newspaper open on his knee and a frown upon his face. Complaining that life without a puzzle was flat and dull, he declared that his mind was rusting in the quiet.

Watson went off to his new life, rich in the one thing that the treasure could never have bought, and Holmes stood alone at the window of Baker Street, watching the rain run down the glass. He knew that sooner or later another strange problem would walk through the door. When it did, he would be perfectly ready for it, and he would greet it as an old and welcome friend.
